choices: The magnet heats the filings so they melt into lines.
The filings line up along the magnet's field.
Static charge from the paper pulls the filings into lines.
Air flowing around the magnet pushes the filings into lines.
correct_answer: The filings line up along the magnet's field.
explanation: A magnet has a magnetic field around it; each filing becomes a tiny magnet and lines up with the field, showing its shape.

distractor_rationales.choice: The magnet heats the filings so they melt into lines.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: magnets act by heating objects

distractor_rationales.choice: Static charge from the paper pulls the filings into lines.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: the pattern comes from electric charge on the paper

distractor_rationales.choice: Air flowing around the magnet pushes the filings into lines.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: magnets act by moving the air

real_world_check: Magnets have fields that extend into space and act on magnetic materials such as iron.

prompt: A pot of water on a stove reaches 100 °C and starts to boil. The burner stays on high, but the water stays at 100 °C until it has boiled away. Which best explains this?
choices: The added energy goes into turning liquid into gas.
The pot gets so hot that it holds the extra heat.
The burner stops heating once the water starts to boil.
correct_answer: The added energy goes into turning liquid into gas.
explanation: While water boils, the energy added breaks particles free from the liquid to form gas instead of raising the temperature.

distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: the reading stops because the thermometer fails

distractor_rationales.choice: The pot gets so hot that it holds the extra heat.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: the pot soaks up the energy instead of the water

distractor_rationales.choice: The burner stops heating once the water starts to boil.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: a stove stops giving energy when water boils

real_world_check: During a change of state, added thermal energy changes the state of a substance rather than its temperature.

prompt: A girl catches two baseballs of the same mass, one thrown slowly and one thrown fast. The fast one stings her hand much more. Which best explains this?
choices: The faster ball brings more energy of motion to your hand.
The slow ball is lighter than the fast ball.
A fast ball heats up in the air and turns as hard as a rock.
Your hand tenses up more when the ball is thrown slowly to you.
correct_answer: The faster ball brings more energy of motion to your hand.
explanation: Kinetic energy grows with speed, so the fast ball carries more energy, which is transferred to the hand when it is caught.

distractor_rationales.choice: The slow ball is lighter than the fast ball.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: a ball that moves faster must have more mass

distractor_rationales.choice: A fast ball heats up in the air and turns as hard as a rock.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: speed makes a ball harder

distractor_rationales.choice: Your hand tenses up more when the ball is thrown slowly to you.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: the sting depends on the catcher, not on the ball's energy

real_world_check: Kinetic energy depends on speed as well as mass; a faster object of the same mass has more kinetic energy.
